title: Tens and ones: why 23 and 23 tens are different
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.title: What does 23 mean in tens and ones?
sections.html:
23 means two tens and three ones: 20 + 3. Imagine 23 loose counters. Put ten in one bundle and ten in another; three counters remain loose.

Nothing new has appeared. The bundles just make the same collection easier to count. This is place value: a digit’s position tells you its value, as OpenStax explains.

sections.title: But what does “23 tens” mean?
sections.html:
23 tens means 23 groups of ten: 23 × 10 = 230. That is different from the number 23, which has only two complete tens.

  • 23: two tens and three ones.
  • 23 tens: twenty-three groups of ten, making 230.
  • 23 tens and 4 ones: 230 + 4 = 234.

The word after the number matters. Twenty-three counters and twenty-three bags of ten counters are rather different deliveries.

sections.title: Why the zero in 30 matters
sections.html:
In 30, the 3 counts tens and the 0 shows no loose ones. Remove the zero and you get 3: just three ones.

Likewise, 23 and 32 use the same digits, but 32 has three tens and two ones. Moving the digits changes the amount.

sections.title: Read the groups, then the number
sections.html:
Try 47: four tens and seven ones. Then try eight ones: no complete tens, just eight loose counters.

Continue with the friendly guide to basic arithmetic when you want another small step.

description: 23 has two tens and three ones, but 23 tens means 230. Use simple bundles to see how place value works and why a zero can change the number.
